questions.q: What does moving up one Snowflake warehouse size (e.g. Small to Medium) roughly do?
options: Adds exactly 10% more compute for the same credit cost
Has no effect on compute, only on storage capacity
Automatically enables multi-cluster mode
Doubles the available compute and doubles the credit-consumption rate
questions.explain: Each Snowflake warehouse size roughly doubles both the compute available and the rate credits are consumed — bigger isn't free, and isn't always faster for a given query.

questions.q: When should you scale up (increase a single warehouse's size) rather than scale out?
options: Whenever storage costs are too high
Never — scaling up is always the wrong choice in Snowflake
When one specific query is genuinely compute- or memory-bound, such as one spilling to disk in Query Profile
When many users are running moderate queries concurrently and queuing behind each other
questions.explain: Scaling up adds more compute to a single warehouse, which helps a genuinely compute/memory-bound query. Concurrency problems from many simultaneous users are better solved by scaling out with a multi-cluster warehouse.

questions.q: What problem does a multi-cluster warehouse (scaling out) solve?
options: Many users running moderate queries at the same time and queuing behind each other
A single query that needs more memory to avoid spilling to disk
A table that needs a clustering key
Slow VPN connections between the client and Snowflake
questions.explain: Multi-cluster warehouses add parallel capacity — additional same-sized clusters — for concurrency, rather than more power for any single query.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which columns in a Query History view help you find expensive or slow queries?
options: The masking policy applied to each column
The role hierarchy depth
Duration and Bytes Scanned
Table name and column count only
questions.explain: Sorting a Query History table by Duration or Bytes Scanned surfaces the queries that are actually worth investigating further in Query Profile.

questions.q: Once an expensive query is identified in Query History, what does this lesson say the next step is?
options: Immediately resize every warehouse in the account to 4X-Large
Grant ACCOUNTADMIN to the user who ran it
Delete the query from history so it doesn't reappear
Open its Query Profile to find the expensive operator node, then decide whether the fix is a better filter, a clustering key, or more compute
questions.explain: This lesson closes the loop back to Query Profile (Lesson 43): find the expensive operator node, then choose the appropriate fix — a filter, a clustering key (Lesson 45), or genuinely more compute.
